# On the Strange Gift of Being Between Things

There's a peculiar comfort in the in-between moments of life, the ones we rarely pause to examine. I'm thinking about that space between waking and sleep, when your mind is still half-dreaming but your eyes are opening to the ceiling of your bedroom. Or that pause in conversation when someone has just asked you a question and you haven't yet answered, when the air holds the question like a soap bubble. Or standing in a doorway—literally between two rooms, belonging fully to neither.

We spend so much of our lives rushing through these liminal spaces as if they're merely transitions, moments to get past on the way to somewhere else. Wake up. Get through the day. Go to bed. But I think there's something worth examining in the texture of these between-times, because they're actually where a lot of living happens, where a lot of truth lives.

I've been thinking about this more since the pandemic, that strange collective pause that forced millions of us into a waiting room of sorts. We were between our old lives and new ones we couldn't yet see. And something interesting happened in that forced stillness—some people discovered they hated their old jobs. Others realized their marriages needed attention. Some found that solitude was exactly what they needed, while others nearly suffocated in it. The between revealed things that the forward momentum had been obscuring.

There's also something about being between ages that strikes me as significant. Adolescence gets a lot of attention as this awkward in-between time, and rightly so—it's genuinely disorienting to be neither child nor adult, when your body is betraying you constantly and your emotions feel like someone else's imported software running on your hardware. But we don't talk enough about being between decades as an adult. The space between thirty and forty, for instance. You're old enough to have made some mistakes but often young enough to change course, still building but maybe beginning to see the shape of what you've built, still ambitious but perhaps more aware of mortality.

I think about people between careers too—that moment when you hand in your resignation letter and before you start the new job. There's a particular species of fear and freedom in that gap. Your identity, which was so firmly tied to what you did for eight hours a day, suddenly becomes unmoored. Who are you when you're not your job? Some people find that terrifying. Others find it liberating. I suspect it depends partly on the person and partly on how much of themselves they'd already surrendered to their work.

There's also something poignant about being between relationships. That period after a significant relationship ends but before you've fully integrated the loss, when you're still sleeping on the same side of the bed out of habit, when their favorite song comes on and you feel the echo of them. And then eventually, one day, you notice you're sleeping in the middle of the bed. You've moved through the between-time without quite noticing it happening. You've arrived on the other side.

I'm interested in the between because it's where we're actually most ourselves, I think. When we're in a defined state—in a job, in a relationship, in a place—we tend to develop a persona that fits that state. We become professional versions of ourselves at work, romantic versions at home, family versions with our parents. These aren't false exactly, but they're curated, edited for context. But in the between-times, there's no audience. There's no role to play because you're not yet in the scene.

That's why airports are such strange spaces. Everyone there is in between. No one quite belongs. You see people at their most unguarded sometimes in airports—more so than in their own homes, maybe, because everyone else is also in transit, also displaced. There's an odd equality in that. The businessman in the expensive suit and the student in ripped jeans and the elderly woman shuffling along in compression socks are all equal in their in-betweenness, all equally far from home and not yet where they're going.

I've read that many creative breakthroughs happen in these threshold spaces. Writers talk about getting their best ideas in the shower—that space between dirty and clean, between the private act of bathing and the public world waiting beyond the door. Mathematicians talk about insights arriving while walking or exercising, when your conscious mind is occupied with something mundane while your unconscious mind is free to make new connections. Artists talk about that space in the beginning of a project where anything is still possible, before the work starts asserting its own demands.

There's something about the between that opens up possibility in a way that defined states don't. When you're firmly inside something—inside a belief system, inside an identity, inside a career—it's harder to see alternatives. The walls are solid. But in the in-between, the walls are more permeable. You can glimpse other possibilities.

I think this is why people fear the between so intensely, actually. We talk about transitions as if they're things to be minimized, brief uncomfortable periods we endure to get to the next stable state. We make plans to escape them. But what we're really afraid of, I suspect, is the freedom that comes with them. As long as you're between things, you could still become almost anything. The moment you commit to the next state, possibilities collapse. You become defined again.

There's grief in that collapse, even when it's a choice you're happy about. I've noticed this with people who've made major life changes. Even when they're relieved to be leaving the old situation—an unhappy marriage, a bad job, a city they hated—there's often a strange melancholy about it. Because the moment of transition, as painful as it might have been, was also a moment of pure possibility. And that's gone now.

I wonder if the ability to exist comfortably in between states is actually a form of maturity. Children need the structures, the clear definitions. A child needs to know they're a student, that they belong to a family, that they have a home. These things are stabilizing. But adults can maybe afford to hold things more lightly, to be okay with uncertainty, to resist the urge to resolve every question into a definitive answer.

There's a Keats concept called "negative capability"—the ability to be in mystery and doubt without reaching for resolution. He was talking about it in the context of poetry, but I think it applies to life too. Our culture pushes us toward positive capability—the drive to solve problems, to reach conclusions, to get to the bottom of things. But maybe some of the richness of living comes from being able to sit with questions, to exist in multiple states at once, to not rush to resolution.

I've been thinking about how language itself resists the in-between. We want nouns, things with clear definitions. We're uncomfortable with prepositions, those small words that indicate position and relationship. We'd rather say "I am happy" than "I am between contentment and longing." We'd rather have a job title than admit we're figuring out what we want to do with our lives. But reality is more prepositions than nouns, isn't it? We're always between things, always in relation to other things, always moving.

The other thought I keep having is about death, and I apologize for the darkness of it, but it seems relevant. Death is, of course, the ultimate between—it's where we all transition from one state to another, from existing to not existing (or to something else, depending on what you believe). And the fact that we don't know what death is, that we can't see past that threshold, is probably why we find it so disturbing. It's the ultimate in-between that we can't resolve. We can't get past it to see what's on the other side.

But maybe that's exactly why we should pay more attention to the smaller in-betweens. They're rehearsals for the big one. They're practice in letting go of definition, in tolerating uncertainty, in accepting that we don't always get to know where we're going before we have to let go of where we were.

I've been thinking too about the between in relationships, not just romantic ones but all of them. There's that early stage of a friendship where you're both presenting curated versions of yourselves, and it's pleasant but not deep. Then if you're lucky, you move through a between-time where the masks slip and you're both vulnerable. And if that works out, you emerge into a deeper friendship where you can be yourselves. But it takes being willing to be in between, to risk the awkwardness of being seen.

The same is true with families, with communities, with any human connection. The between is where real intimacy becomes possible. It's uncomfortable—you might say something that makes things weird, you might be rejected. But growth happens in that discomfort.

I think perhaps what I'm trying to say is that we've been taught to be afraid of the wrong things. We've been taught to fear uncertainty, to fear being caught between states, to fear not knowing. And so we rush through these in-between moments, barely pausing to notice them, missing the texture of them. We're like someone rushing through a cathedral without looking up, so focused on getting to the other door that we miss the light coming through the stained glass.

The between is where we're alive in a particular way. It's where we haven't yet solidified into who we'll be. Where we can still change our minds. Where mystery lives. It's uncomfortable and it's terrifying and it's also, I think, where the best things are possible.

I don't have a tidy conclusion here. But I think if I could tell my younger self anything, it would be this: slow down in the in-between moments. They're not obstacles to your real life. They're part of your real life, maybe the most important part. The moments when you're between jobs are moments of potential. The time between ending a relationship and beginning a new one is time to know yourself. The pause before you speak is where your most honest words live. The space between sleep and waking is where your unconscious mind shows you things. The threshold is sacred.

We're always between things, always in transition, always moving from what we were toward what we might become. Learning to exist gracefully in that movement, to see it as the point rather than as a means to a point, might be the closest thing we have to wisdom.
